new_statements.quote: El acento es un signo que se utiliza para enfatizar la intensidad de la pronunciación en alguna sílaba de las palabras. Se acentuarán todas las palabras en aquellas sílabas que tengan mayor intensidad en agudas y esdrújulas, respetando las siete variantes que existen en la lengua tutunakú, excepto las palabras graves. [...] Las palabras tetrasílabas, trisílabas o bisílabas con intensidad de voz en la penúltima sílaba no se acentuarán y se les conocerá como palabras graves. [...] Las palabras monosílabas no se acentuarán. [...] Se acentuarán todas las palabras tetrasílabas y trisílabas que lleven la intensidad acentual en la antepenúltima sílaba, a estas se les conocerá como palabras esdrújulas.
new_statements.translation: The accent is a sign used to mark the intensity of pronunciation on some syllable of a word. All words will carry a written accent on the syllable with greatest intensity when they are oxytone (final-stressed) or proparoxytone (antepenult-stressed), respecting the seven variants that exist in the Tutunakú language, except paroxytone words. [...] Four-, three- or two-syllable words with the intensity on the penultimate syllable will not be accented and will be known as 'graves'. [...] Monosyllables are not accented. [...] All four- and three-syllable words with the accentual intensity on the antepenultimate syllable will be accented; these will be known as 'esdrújulas'.
new_statements.citation: Instituto Nacional de Lenguas Indígenas (INALI). 2017. Xalimakgatsokgni tutunakú / Norma de escritura de la lengua tutunakú (totonaco). México: INALI. 170 pp. (PDF created Nov 2017; norm elaborated in workshops 2003-2015 with bilingual teachers from Puebla and Veracruz, incl. sessions in Zihuateutla and Pantepec).

(4461-4463, p. 131-132), 'Las palabras monosíl…
new_statements.relation_note: Treats Totonac as a stress language with a written acute accent; no mention of tone.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Orthographic convention, pan-Totonac: word stress ('intensidad') may fall on the final, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable; penultimate stress is treated as the unmarked default (no written accent), final and antepenultimate stress are written with an acute accent. Examples given: final stress on words ending in a vowel (lakchawá, katsí, lhtukú — vowel length is not written in this orthography) or in m, n, t, y, lh (takám, puskát, wankgólh); penult stress in lakgastapu, tlakgama, statu, kuxi; antepenult in wápapa, palókgoyo, táskuyu. No phonological rule of stress placement is stated.
new_statements.exceptions: monosyllables never accented; 'respetando las siete variantes' (variants may differ)
new_statements.identity_note: Prescriptive orthographic norm 'válida para todas las variantes lingüísticas del tutunakú' (INALI treats Totonac as one language with 7 variants; Tecpatlán/Zihuateutla fall in its 'central del norte'/'del río Necaxa' area, and Zihuateutla municipality is listed among participating communities). It is not a description of Tecpatlán Totonac and its example words are not attributed to any variety.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3 languoid page tecp1235 (Hammarström et al.), with linked reference records 700656 (Beck 2025 'Totonacan languages', Mouton) and 569683 (Campbell et al. 2022 ElCat); Glottolog reference search q=Tecpatlán

sources.citation: García-Vega, Michelle. 2022. Morphology of Zihuateutla Totonac. PhD dissertation, University of Alberta (Scholaris hdl 123456789/74436). Sister Northern Totonac language, Zihuateutla municipality (the municipality Tecpatlán lies).
sources.note: NOT about Tecpatlán (0 mentions). For Zihuateutla Totonac, §2.2 'Stress' pp. 47-53: 'stress in ZT is fairly regular and predictable, falling on the ultimate or the penultimate syllable for all lexical classes.. stress the penultimate syllable in words ending in a light syllable.. and stress falls on the ultimate syllable of words ending in a heavy syllable that is, words ending in a long vowel or closed syllable' (p. 53); exceptions: agentive nominalizer attracts stress, deictic adverbs final, stem-final verbs final; auditory judgments of citation forms.

sources.citation: Beck, David. 2008. Ideophones, adverbs, and predicate qualification in Upper Necaxa Totonac. IJAL 74(1): 1-46 (fn. 2, p. 2) — already held by the project from the patl1234 check
sources.note: Stress section (§2.3, p. 15) is for Upper Necaxa only. Fn. 2: Tecpatlán 'differs significantly from the Totonac of Patla and Chicontla both lexically and phonologically.. so it seems best to exclude Tecpatlán from Upper Necaxa Totonac' — i.e. the UNT stress statement is explicitly not claimed for Tecpatlán.

sources.citation: Beck, David. 2007. ISO 639-3 Request for New Language Code Element: Tecpatlán Totonac (tcw), associated with CR 2006-085. 5 pp.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Location (village of Tecpatlán plus possibly two smaller communities, valley of a tributary of the Necaxa River), ~540 speakers per INEGI, community also bilingual in Nahuatl; 'Knowledge from published sources' left blank; written literature: 'none'; closest language: 'unknown'.

sources.citation: Beck, David (with Yvonne Lam). 2006. ISO 639-3 Change Request 2006-085: split [tot] Patla-Chicontla Totonac into Upper Necaxa Totonac [tku] and Tecpatlán Totonac [tcw]. SIL International ISO 639-3 Registration Authority, 7 pp.
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Only Tecpatlán-specific phonological remarks anywhere: Tecpatlán 'has also undergone a shift of /w/ to /b/', shares lenition of *q to glottal stop with Upper Necaxa but 'retains /q/ in at least some lexical items'; many lexical differences; Beck 'recorded a short text in Tecpatlán' in 2006 (unpublished).

sources.citation: Wycliffe Bible Translators. 1999. Xasāstiʼ testamento (Xatze tachihuīn ixpālacata Jesucristo) [El Nuevo Testamento en el totonaco de Patla y Chicontla]. México: La Liga Bíblica / WBT. Digital text: eBible.org id tkuNT (CC BY-NC-ND), 27 books, USFM.
sources.note: Primary text only (no preface, no orthography note in the digital edition). The practical orthography writes vowel length with macrons (ā ē ī ō ū) and laryngealization with an apostrophe but does NOT mark stress: across 159,364 word tokens the only acute-accented forms (4,493 tokens, 268 types) are Spanish names and loans (Jesús, Espíritu, ixángeles, quilī'apóstol…). Hence not even wordlist-level stress data.
